name: Pedro Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six and on the train to Tideline Foodservice by seven. We supply school canteens, care homes and restaurants across the region, and I buy the frozen and dry goods: about 1,400 lines from sixty-odd suppliers. First hour is phone calls, because the Friday-night price changes land by Monday and I like to hear a supplier's voice when the news is bad. Then I meet Odile (our planner) about what's running low, and I haggle. I love that bit. What wears me out is the squeeze from the big chains, who want the same quality for less every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the hype people were selling us was nonsense anyway. At work I'd shrug and say the software does what the software did before. To friends I'd say a phone call still beats a dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays mine, and that's a relief. But it also means the pressure I already carry doesn't go away. The chains keep pushing prices down, and our margins are thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep the Friday calls with my sixty suppliers and keep Odile's reorder meeting. Maybe I'd put an extra 400 a month towards the mortgage, since we've got room and the rate resets next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit tense, not scared. It's the old worry, the margin worry, and I've lived with it for ten years. Nothing new in it, which is a kind of comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the chains squeeze you already. Who feels that squeeze first at Tideline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Odile and the warehouse crew feel it first. When the chains squeeze us, we squeeze the overtime. Last winter the night shift lost two hours a week each, and I felt rotten about it. I sit in the union meetings as a friend of the warehouse side, and I hear it straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids that night, if they asked whether your job is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Sami (my eldest) that Dad's job is safe, and that Dad has a plan if it isn't. Nobody ever lost a pallet of frozen peas because of a spreadsheet, but I've lost three because a supplier wouldn't pick up the phone. Rita, who's eight, would just ask if we're still going to the coast in August.

say: I'd say the **hype** was nonsense and a phone call still beats a dashboard.
I'd tell the warehouse crew that **nothing** changes for them either.
think: My job is safe, but the **margin squeeze** from the big chains stays.
The mortgage rate resets next spring, and that worries me more than AI.
do: Keep the **Friday calls** with all sixty suppliers and the reorder meeting with Odile.
Put an extra **400 a month** towards the mortgage.
feel: A bit **tense**, but it's an old worry, so it's familiar.
S0.quote: Nobody ever lost a pallet of frozen peas because of a spreadsheet, but I've lost three because a supplier wouldn't pick up the phone.
fieldNote: Pedro's worry is the **chains**, not AI, so calm would be wrong while his margins and the mortgage rate stay unsettled.
Shows his loyalty to the warehouse side early, a thread that runs through every scenario.

steps.text: Keep the Friday phone calls with all sixty suppliers
Pay an extra 400 a month towards the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's another round of cost-cutting wearing a clever hat. To friends I'd say someone has to be accountable when a buying decision goes wrong, and software can't be. Online I'd say this needs rules, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think they'll go after my team first. Checking quotes, matching invoices, flagging low stock: that's the junior half of my department, and it's exactly what these tools do. They'll say it frees people up, and then the headcount quietly drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Brandt, our purchasing director, and push for a written promise that nobody loses a job to software without retraining. I'd go to the next union meeting and ask for it there too. I still won't touch the tools myself in the first year. Maybe I'd sit with Odile while she tries one, just to understand what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly. I've given sixteen years to this company, and I'm treated as a cost to be trimmed. There's some fear in there too, because I know I'm digging in my heels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would software take first, and how do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quote checking and invoice matching, definitely. Our two junior buyers, Kasia and Dev, spend half their week on that. If it goes to software, I'd have to explain to them why they're being asked to 'upskill'. That's a hard meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. What would make you try one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try one only if the union had a seat in how it's used and I could see the reasoning behind each number. A black box choosing my suppliers? No. I'd want to see why it picked a supplier, the way I'd explain it to Brandt.

say: It's **cost-cutting** with a clever hat, and someone must stay accountable for buying decisions.
This needs **rules**, written down, before the first junior buyer goes.
think: They'll take the **junior half** of my team first, matching invoices and checking quotes.
I'm digging in my heels, and I know it, but I **don't trust** a black box.
do: Ask Brandt for a **written promise** of retraining before any job goes.
Raise it at the next **union meeting** and sit with Odile while she tries a tool.
feel: **Angry** at being treated as a cost, with a little fear underneath.
S1.quote: A black box choosing my suppliers? No. I'd want to see why it picked a supplier, the way I'd explain it to Brandt.
fieldNote: Pedro **resists** the tools but says it plainly, which fits his resistant profile and stays honest rather than defensive.
His first move is a **collective** one: written promises and the union, not learning the tools.

steps.text: Ask Brandt for a written retraining promise
Raise job protection at the union meeting
Sit with Odile while she tries a buying tool
Keep running the supplier calls myself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need government in the room today. To friends I'd say this is exactly what unions and regulation are for. Online I'd say whoever profits from this must pay for the people it throws out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. Buying is thinking work: reading markets, weighing offers, trusting a voice. If a machine does it all better and cheaper, I'm in the first group to go, and my master's degree won't help. That's the blunt truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd freeze everything big: no holiday, no kitchen extension. I'd move six months of cash into the safe account. I'd go hard at the union and the council, asking for retraining money and some kind of income support. In year one I'd also finally learn one of these tools, because pride won't pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. It's the speed. Two years isn't enough time for Brandt to make a plan, let alone for the government to. I'd be lying awake with the mortgage figure in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What would you say to Lucia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lucia (my partner, a primary teacher) that her job is safer, and that we need to live on her pay if we have to. Then I'd say we've got money in the bank, which is true, but it's not an answer. I'd say we'd be fine for a year and I don't know after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots about three years after, does the fact that your work is desk-based change how you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The desk work goes first, and that's me. The robots come about three years later, so the warehouse crew get a bit longer, and that's a bitter thing: I'd lose my job first and they'd lose theirs second. If my own job goes, my own job goes, and that doesn't make me feel safe because they have three more years.

say: We need **government** in the room now, and whoever profits must pay for the people displaced.
This is exactly what **unions** and regulation are for.
think: Buying is thinking work, so I'm in the **first group** to go, degree or not.
Two years is too short for Brandt or the government to make a **plan**.
do: Freeze big spending and move **six months** of cash into the safe account.
Press the union and the council for **retraining** money, and finally learn one tool.
feel: **Frightened** and sick about the speed, awake at night with the mortgage figure.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time for Brandt to make a plan, let alone for the government to.
fieldNote: Pedro's **cushion** keeps him at alarmed rather than panicked: he has a plan, just not a long one.
The warehouse crew get three more years than he does, which he finds **bitter** rather than comforting.

steps.text: Move six months of cash into the safe account
Cancel the kitchen extension and the summer holiday
Press the council for retraining money and income support
Learn one buying tool before the year ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this gives us time to do it properly, if we use it. To friends I'd say I'm worried, but not panicking. Online I'd say governments have five years to get a retraining scheme built, and I'll be nagging them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to change my life, if I start now. It's still my job at stake, though, and I know I'll be one of the early ones. I'd rather know and be afraid than not know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd study. Probably something in supply contracts or procurement law, evenings, because a human who understands what a deal means is harder to replace. I'd also get the mortgage down hard, maybe a lump sum from the bonus. And I'd keep pushing the union to bargain a retraining clause into the next agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one. Frightened, yes, but also determined. Five years feels like a fight I can actually have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years than with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be in survival mode, selling things. With five, I'd be rebuilding: courses, a different role, maybe training buyers in the warehouse side to move into negotiating. I'd want the time to be real, not just a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from Tideline in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From Tideline I'd want paid study days and a promise that they'll move people into new roles before they let them go. I'd tell Brandt directly: if Tideline can afford the software, Tideline can afford our retraining. Sixteen years of loyalty should buy that.

say: Five years is enough to do this **properly**, if governments build a retraining scheme.
I'm worried but **not panicking**, and I'll keep nagging.
think: Five years can change my life if I **start now**, though my job is still on the line.
I'd rather know and be **afraid** than not know.
do: Study **procurement law** in the evenings, because a human who understands a deal is harder to replace.
Push the union to bargain a **retraining clause** into the next agreement.
feel: Frightened but **determined**, because five years feels like a fight I can have.
S3.quote: If Tideline can afford the software, Tideline can afford our retraining. Sixteen years of loyalty should buy that.
fieldNote: The extra time moves Pedro from **survival** mode to rebuilding, which is a clear shift in what he says he'd do.
He frames retraining as something Tideline **owes** him after sixteen years.

steps.text: Study procurement law in the evenings for two years
Put the next bonus as a lump sum on the mortgage
Push the union to bargain a retraining clause

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a decade gives everyone room, and I'd be almost easy about it. To friends I'd say it's still wrong that so few people are planning. Online I'd say governments should start now, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'll be 53 when it arrives. That's old enough that I'd rather have retrained by then, or be close to a lower-stress job. It's not my own fear that bothers me most at that distance, it's my kids' working lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Tideline and use the time well. I'd learn one tool in a couple of years when it's proven, finish paying down the mortgage, and maybe move to a role training the next generation of buyers. I'd also help Sami and Rita choose studies that need a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but not calm. There's a kind of grief in it, that the thing I'm good at will be done by a machine. I'll be proud and a bit sad in the same breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What changes for you and for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my children it changes everything. I'd steer my son Sami towards the care professions or skilled trades, things where a person stays in the room. I'd tell Rita to study what she likes and be good with people. I won't be pushing them to be buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in feeling too relaxed with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the risk, and I know it about myself. I could drift for eight years and then panic. So I'd write down checkpoints: a course by year three, a role change by year six, a mortgage cleared by 2033.

say: A decade gives everyone **room**, but too few people are planning.
Governments should start **now**, not in year nine.
think: I'll be **53** when it arrives, so I'd rather be retrained or near a calmer role.
What bothers me most is my **kids'** working lives, more than my own fear.
do: Learn one proven tool in a couple of years and clear the **mortgage by 2033**.
Move towards a role **training** the next generation of buyers.
feel: Calmer, but with a quiet **grief** that a machine will do what I'm good at.
S4.quote: I'd steer my son Sami towards the care professions or skilled trades, things where a person stays in the room.
fieldNote: Pedro **resists** change and says so: he'd set checkpoints because he knows he might drift for eight years.
His concern shifts to his **children's** careers, a change from the earlier, more personal scenarios.

steps.text: Learn one proven buying tool by year three
Move into training new buyers around year six
Guide Sami and Rita towards studies that need a person

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The ten-year one worries me least. The two-year one is the nightmare, because the desk work goes first and there's no time for Brandt, the union or the government to do anything. What would help is a real retraining guarantee, written into law and into our contract, and income support for the gap. Also some honesty from companies, so I'm not the last to know.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me get called old-fashioned for resisting these tools. I'm not afraid of machines, I'm afraid of who decides how they're used. Ask me again in a year and I may have changed my mind about the tool part.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of machines, I'm afraid of who decides how they're used.
portrait: Pedro is a 43-year-old senior **senior buyer** at Tideline Foodservice, with a partner, two children and a mortgage.
He is progressive, **union-minded** and resistant to AI tools, and he trusts phone calls and people over dashboards.
He'd stay calm-ish only if nothing changes; as AGI nears he turns to **collective action** and retraining claims on his employer.
His cushion keeps him from panic, and he worries most about **his children's** working lives.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario, because desk work goes first and nobody has time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining guarantee** in law and contract, plus income support for the gap and honesty from employers.
